$comment: Shared AHP conformance fixtures. The TypeScript implementation in my-app/lib/ahp and the Python one in services/analysis/app/domain/ahp.py are both tested against this file, so they cannot disagree about a weight or a consistency ratio. Tolerances are absolute. Adding a case here obliges both sides.

cases.name: notebook-weights-round-trip
cases.why: A consistent matrix built from the Tana River notebook's AHP weights must return them exactly. This is the ground truth for the eigenvector: there is one right answer and it is known in advance.

cases.name: saaty-textbook-3x3
cases.why: Saaty's published example. The expected values are from the literature, not from either implementation, so agreeing with them is independent evidence rather than agreeing with ourselves.

cases.name: all-equal
cases.why: Every comparison equal must give equal weights and perfect consistency, at any order.

cases.name: two-criteria-cannot-be-inconsistent
cases.why: RI is 0 at order 2. Dividing by it gives NaN or Infinity and rejects a matrix that is correct by construction. Both implementations must special-case this rather than divide.

cases.name: single-criterion
cases.why: Order 1 is degenerate but legal: one criterion carries all the weight.

cases.name: cyclic-preference-is-refused
cases.why: A strongly beats B, B strongly beats C, C strongly beats A. Not a close call, impossible. Catching this is the entire reason the consistency ratio is computed rather than the weights taken on trust.

cases.name: mildly-inconsistent-but-usable
cases.why: The realistic case: judgements that do not line up perfectly but stay inside the threshold. Both sides must accept it and agree on the ordering.

invalid.name: not-reciprocal
invalid.why: Reciprocity is what makes it an AHP matrix at all.

invalid.name: zero-comparison
invalid.why: A zero is not a weak preference, it is a broken matrix; its eigenvector means nothing.
